skill.hx.neuro.approach.title: Localising from the history alone
skill.hx.neuro.approach.oneLine: Onset, course, and distribution answer WHERE before you touch the patient
skill.hx.neuro.approach.why: In neurology the history often localises the lesion before the examination confirms it. Three questions, onset, course over time, and distribution of the symptom, do most of that work.

asks.text: How did it start: sudden, over hours, over days, or gradually over months?
Has it stayed the same, improved, worsened, or come and gone?
Exactly which part of the body, and does it cross the midline?
Any weakness, numbness, visual change, speech difficulty, or loss of consciousness alongside it?
Headache, and if so, is it the worst of their life or different from their usual pattern?

teach.heading: Onset tells you the mechanism
teach.note: A useful rule of thumb: the faster the onset, the more likely it is vascular; the slower, the more likely it is structural or degenerative.

teach.heading: Course over time is the second axis

points.d: Typical of a vascular event once the initial insult is over.
Recurrent small vascular events, or relapsing demyelination.
A growing structural lesion, or a progressive degenerative process.
Myasthenia, or a metabolic derangement.

teach.heading: Distribution: does it cross the midline
teach.body: A single, well-demarcated body part, or a whole side of the body, suggests a lesion in the central nervous system on the OPPOSITE side. Symptoms that cross the midline, or that follow a specific nerve or root rather than a whole limb, point to the peripheral nervous system instead.

teach.heading: What travels alongside the main complaint

points.t: Weakness or numbness on the same side as a visual or speech problem.
points.d: Suggests one cortical territory, usually one vascular distribution.

points.t: A brief loss of consciousness before or after the event.
points.d: Raises seizure as well as syncope; ask what the patient, and any witness, actually saw.

points.t: A headache that is the worst of the patient's life, or reaches maximum intensity within seconds (thunderclap).
points.d: Needs subarachnoid haemorrhage actively excluded, not assumed away.

teach.note: Ask for a witness account whenever there was any alteration of consciousness. What the patient remembers and what actually happened are often two different histories.

pitfalls: Not asking exactly how fast a symptom developed, which is the single most useful localising question in neurology.
Missing a 'worst headache of my life', which needs subarachnoid haemorrhage actively excluded.
Taking the patient's own account of a blackout at face value without asking a witness what was actually seen.

probes.q: A weakness developed over seconds. What category of cause does that suggest?
probes.a: A vascular event, such as a haemorrhage or embolic stroke.

probes.q: Symptoms confined to one whole side of the body. Central or peripheral nervous system?
probes.a: Central, and on the side OPPOSITE the symptoms, because of the crossing of major motor and sensory pathways.

probes.q: A patient describes the worst headache of their life, reaching full intensity within seconds. What must be actively excluded?
probes.a: Subarachnoid haemorrhage.

rubric.text: Establishes the speed of onset
Establishes the course over time
Screens for red-flag headache or sudden severe symptoms

skill.exam.neuro.higher_mental.title: Higher mental functions: consciousness, orientation, memory and speech
skill.exam.neuro.higher_mental.oneLine: The GCS, orientation in three domains, three types of memory, and the six-domain language screen
skill.exam.neuro.higher_mental.why: Higher mental function is examined before anything else, because an unreliable historian changes how you interpret every symptom that follows. A structured screen, level of consciousness, orientation, memory, calculation, and language, turns a vague impression of 'confused' into a testable, reproducible finding.

steps.text: Note the level of consciousness first, in the patient's own words if possible, and score it on the Glasgow Coma Scale (eye, verbal, motor) if there is any doubt.
Test orientation in three domains: time (year, season, month, date, day), place (country, state, city, hospital, floor), and person.
Test immediate memory (digit span, forward and backward) and recent memory (three objects, recalled after about 5 minutes of unrelated conversation).
Test calculation: serial sevens from 100, or spelling a word backward.
Screen language across its domains: spontaneous fluency, comprehension of a command, repetition of a phrase, naming two objects, reading, and writing a sentence.

skill.exam.neuro.higher_mental.normal: Fully conscious (GCS 15), oriented to time, place and person, normal digit span (7 plus or minus 2), recalls 3/3 objects at 5 minutes, completes serial sevens, and fluent, comprehending, intact speech across all six domains.
skill.exam.neuro.higher_mental.abnormal: Any reduction in GCS; disorientation in any domain; an inability to register or recall; errors in calculation; or a defect in fluency, comprehension, repetition, naming, reading or writing.
skill.exam.neuro.higher_mental.significance: The GCS gives a reproducible number that any clinician can trend over time; a falling score is itself the emergency. Which domains of memory and language fail, and which are spared, localises: recent memory loss with intact remote memory points to the medial temporal lobe, while the pattern of fluency, comprehension and repetition failure maps onto Broca's, Wernicke's or a conduction lesion.

teach.heading: The Glasgow Coma Scale, scored not just described
teach.body: Score each of the three domains separately, then sum them.

rows: Spontaneous / to voice / to pain / none
Oriented / confused / inappropriate words / sounds / none
Obeys / localises pain / withdraws / flexion (decorticate) / extension (decerebrate) / none

teach.note: Maximum 15, minimum 3. A GCS of 8 or less is, by definition, coma. In an intubated patient the verbal score is recorded as 'VT' rather than forced into a number.

teach.heading: Naming the level of consciousness precisely

rows: Rouses easily, then promptly falls back asleep if left alone
Needs a mild-to-moderate stimulus to rouse, and is slow once awake
Rouses only to a vigorous or painful stimulus, with no meaningful verbal or motor response
Cannot be roused by any stimulus; no awareness, no voluntary movement, no sleep-wake cycle
Alert enough to be roused, but confused, restless and often inattentive or hallucinating; may be reversible

teach.note: Prefer describing the actual responsiveness, or the GCS number, over a single label like 'drowsy': the label means different things to different observers, the number does not.

teach.heading: Three kinds of memory, and where each one lives

rows: Digit span forward and backward, normal 7 plus or minus 2
Three unrelated objects, recalled after about 5 minutes
The patient's own fund of information: schooling, major life and world events

teach.note: Recent memory loss with a preserved fund of remote information is the classic early pattern in a medial temporal process; when it comes with confabulation, think Korsakoff's psychosis.

teach.heading: Reading an aphasia off three simple bedside tests
teach.body: Score comprehension, repetition and fluency as intact or impaired, then read off the type.
teach.note: Test comprehension, repetition and fluency first, in that order; only once those three are characterised does it make sense to go on and check reading, writing and naming.

teach.heading: Aphasia is not dysarthria
teach.body: Aphasia is a disorder of LANGUAGE, from a dominant-hemisphere cortical lesion, and it also disturbs reading and writing. Dysarthria is a disorder of the motor production of speech, usually from a brainstem, cerebellar or neuromuscular problem, and it comes with other bulbar signs such as dysphagia rather than a reading or writing defect. A slurred, hard-to-understand patient can have either, and the distinction changes where you look for the lesion.

pitfalls: Labelling a patient 'confused' without recording GCS or testing all three orientation domains separately.
Testing recall immediately instead of after several minutes of unrelated conversation, which makes recent memory look falsely intact.
Calling slurred speech 'aphasia' without checking comprehension, repetition and fluency, and so missing a dysarthria instead.
Skipping calculation and writing because the patient 'seems fine' in conversation, and missing a mild dominant parietal deficit.

probes.q: What GCS score defines coma?
probes.a: 8 or less.

probes.q: A patient recalls 0 of 3 objects at 5 minutes but can describe events from 20 years ago in detail. Which memory system is affected, and what does that localise to?
probes.a: Recent (short-term) memory is impaired with remote memory preserved, pointing to the hippocampus and medial temporal structures.

probes.q: A patient speaks fluently but the sentences make no sense, and they cannot follow a simple two-step command. Comprehension and repetition are both impaired. What type of aphasia is this, and roughly where is the lesion?
probes.a: Wernicke's (receptive) aphasia, from a lesion in the inferior division of the dominant middle cerebral artery territory (posterior superior temporal region).

probes.q: Distinguish aphasia from dysarthria at the bedside.
probes.a: Aphasia is a disorder of language content, from a dominant cerebral lesion, and also impairs reading and writing; dysarthria is a disorder of the motor production of speech, usually of brainstem/neuromuscular origin, with language itself, and reading/writing, intact, but often accompanied by dysphagia.

rubric.text: Records or scores level of consciousness explicitly
Tests all three orientation domains
Tests immediate and recent memory with an appropriate delay
Screens comprehension, repetition and fluency before labelling a speech disorder

skill.exam.neuro.cn1_2.title: CN I and II: smell, acuity, fields, colour vision and the fundus
skill.exam.neuro.cn1_2.oneLine: Olfactory nerve first, then the four-part optic nerve exam
skill.exam.neuro.cn1_2.why: The olfactory and optic nerves are the two cranial nerves that never pass through the brainstem, so a normal exam here does not clear the brainstem the way a normal CN III to XII exam does. The optic nerve exam is done in four separate parts, and each one has its own differential.

steps.text: CN I: rule out nasal blockage first. With eyes closed, occlude one nostril and present a familiar, non-irritant smell (coffee, peppermint, soap) to the other; ask the patient to detect, then name it. Repeat for the other side, testing the suspected abnormal side first.
Never use ammonia or another irritant: it stimulates the trigeminal nerve directly and gives a false-positive response even with no sense of smell at all.
CN II, visual acuity: test each eye separately, corrected if the patient wears glasses, using a Snellen chart at 6 m (or finger counting if no chart is available).
CN II, visual fields: confrontation testing at arm's length, one eye at a time, bringing a target in from each of the four quadrants.
CN II, colour vision: an Ishihara chart, each eye separately.
CN II, fundus: direct ophthalmoscopy in a dim room, following the red reflex to the disc, then examining all four quadrants and the macula.

skill.exam.neuro.cn1_2.normal: Smell detected and identified equally on both sides; visual acuity 6/6 (or corrected to it); full visual fields to confrontation; correct colour plates identified; a sharp, pink disc with a normal cup, and normal vessels and macula.
skill.exam.neuro.cn1_2.abnormal: Anosmia (uni- or bilateral); reduced acuity; any visual field defect; colour vision errors; papilloedema, optic atrophy, or retinopathy on the fundus.
skill.exam.neuro.cn1_2.significance: The SITE of a visual field defect maps precisely onto where in the visual pathway the lesion sits, which is one of the most reliable localising findings in the whole nervous system. Papilloedema means raised intracranial pressure until proven otherwise.

teach.heading: Anosmia is not always a nose problem
teach.body: Local causes (rhinitis is the most common of all, plus heavy smoking) far outnumber neurological ones, but persistent, otherwise-unexplained anosmia is worth pursuing.

points.d: Anosmia with optic atrophy in one eye and papilloedema in the other, from a frontal lobe tumour compressing one olfactory tract while raising pressure generally.
Parkinsonism, head trauma, meningitis, and as an early feature that can precede the motor signs of several neurodegenerative diseases.

teach.heading: Visual field defects localise the lesion along the pathway
teach.body: Work from the retina backward: where the defect straddles the midline (bitemporal) versus stays on one side (homonymous) is the first branch point.

rows: Total loss of vision in that eye

teach.note: A chiasmal lesion (classically a pituitary tumour) is the one that gives a bitemporal pattern; everything behind the chiasm gives a homonymous pattern on the side opposite the lesion.

teach.heading: Grading papilloedema
teach.body:
Papilloedema is disc swelling from raised intracranial pressure, and it progresses through recognisable stages: blurring of the nasal disc margin first, then circumferential blurring, then obscuration of one or more vessels crossing the disc margin, and finally obscuration of all disc vessels.

Causes span space-occupying lesions, diffuse cerebral oedema, blocked CSF flow (hydrocephalus), reduced CSF reabsorption (meningitis, venous sinus disease, Guillain-Barre's raised CSF protein), and systemic causes such as malignant hypertension.

teach.heading: Colour vision is not just a party trick
teach.body: Congenital red-green defects are X-linked, so they overwhelmingly affect men. Acquired colour vision loss occurs in macular and optic nerve disease, and with certain drugs, ethambutol, chloroquine and digitalis among them, which is exactly why colour vision is checked on ethambutol.

pitfalls: Using ammonia or another irritant to test smell, which stimulates the trigeminal nerve and gives a false result.
Testing visual fields without comparing both eyes to each other, missing a subtle quadrantanopia.
Skipping the red reflex step and 'hunting' for the disc, which usually means giving up before finding it.
Calling a field defect bitemporal without actually testing both temporal fields separately.

probes.q: Why should ammonia never be used to test the olfactory nerve?
probes.a: It directly stimulates trigeminal nerve endings in the nasal mucosa, so even a patient with no sense of smell will report detecting it.

probes.q: A patient has bitemporal hemianopia. Where is the lesion?
probes.a: At the optic chiasm, classically from a pituitary lesion compressing the crossing nasal fibres.

probes.q: Right homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing. Localise it, and explain why the macula is spared.
probes.a: A lesion of the left occipital (calcarine) cortex; the macula is spared because it has a separate, dual blood supply (posterior and middle cerebral arteries), so an isolated posterior cerebral artery infarct can leave the macular representation intact.

probes.q: What does papilloedema on fundoscopy require you to actively consider, and name two broad categories of cause.
probes.a: Raised intracranial pressure, from causes including a space-occupying lesion (tumour, abscess, haemorrhage), blocked CSF outflow (hydrocephalus), or reduced CSF reabsorption (meningitis, venous sinus thrombosis, or the raised CSF protein of Guillain-Barre syndrome).

rubric.text: Tests each nostril separately with a non-irritant substance
Tests visual fields by confrontation in all four quadrants, each eye
Follows the red reflex and examines all four quadrants plus macula

skill.exam.neuro.cn3_4_6.title: CN III, IV, VI: eyelids, eye movements and pupils
skill.exam.neuro.cn3_4_6.oneLine: One H-shaped test covers three nerves; the pupil tells you medical from surgical
skill.exam.neuro.cn3_4_6.why: These three nerves move the eye, and are tested together because a single ocular movement usually depends on more than one of them. Whether the pupil is involved is the single fact that separates a IIIrd nerve palsy that needs urgent imaging from one that can be watched.

steps.text: Inspect the eyelids for ptosis and the eyes at rest for a squint or abnormal position.
Ask the patient to follow your finger through an H-shaped path about 60 cm from their face, watching for restricted movement in any direction and asking about diplopia at each extreme.
Test the direct and consensual light reflex in each eye with a torch, and the accommodation reflex by having the patient look from a distant to a near object.
Look for nystagmus at the extremes of gaze, holding each position for several seconds.

skill.exam.neuro.cn3_4_6.normal: No ptosis, eyes parallel at rest, full smooth movement in all directions with no diplopia, pupils equal and briskly reactive to light and accommodation, no nystagmus.
skill.exam.neuro.cn3_4_6.abnormal: Ptosis; a squint or restricted movement in the distribution of one nerve; a sluggish, unequal, or non-reactive pupil; sustained nystagmus.
skill.exam.neuro.cn3_4_6.significance: The pupil decides urgency in a IIIrd nerve palsy: because parasympathetic fibres run on the outside of the nerve, a compressive lesion (aneurysm, tumour, uncal herniation) hits them early and dilates the pupil, while a microvascular (diabetic) infarct spares the centre-running pupillary fibres and leaves the pupil normal.

teach.heading: Which nerve does which movement

rows: Ptosis, a dilated pupil, and a 'down and out' eye from unopposed lateral rectus and superior oblique
Defective downward gaze in adduction; the patient tilts the head to the opposite side to compensate
Failure of lateral gaze, a convergent squint, diplopia worse on looking to the affected side

teach.heading: Pupil-sparing versus pupil-involving IIIrd nerve palsy
teach.body: The parasympathetic fibres to the pupil travel on the outer surface of the IIIrd nerve, supplied by their own small vessels. A compressive ('surgical') lesion from outside, a posterior communicating artery aneurysm above all, damages those outer fibres early and dilates the pupil. An ischaemic ('medical') lesion, as in longstanding diabetes, affects the core of the nerve first and typically spares the pupil.
teach.note: A new IIIrd nerve palsy WITH a dilated, poorly reactive pupil is a neurosurgical emergency until an aneurysm is excluded; a pupil-sparing IIIrd nerve palsy in a diabetic can usually be observed.

teach.heading: Ptosis: work out which muscle, then which cause

rows: Ptosis with a large, sluggish pupil
IIIrd nerve infarct, myasthenia gravis, or a myopathy
Ptosis that worsens through the day or with sustained upgaze

teach.note: Bilateral ptosis suggests a systemic or neuromuscular cause (myasthenia, bilateral Horner's, myopathy); unilateral ptosis points to a local nerve or sympathetic-pathway lesion on that side.

teach.heading: Reading the light reflex
teach.body:
The light reflex has four neurons: retina to both pretectal nuclei (crossing partially), pretectal nucleus to both Edinger-Westphal nuclei (this is why light in ONE eye constricts BOTH pupils), Edinger-Westphal to the ciliary ganglion via the IIIrd nerve, and ciliary ganglion to the sphincter pupillae.

Because the reflex is wired to both sides, comparing the direct and consensual response in each eye localises the defect to the afferent (retina/optic nerve) or efferent (IIIrd nerve) limb.

pitfalls: Not commenting on the pupil in a IIIrd nerve palsy, which is the single finding that decides whether urgent imaging is needed.
Testing eye movements without asking about diplopia, missing an early, subtle palsy before it is visible.
Missing a compensatory head tilt, which is the presenting clue in a IVth nerve palsy.

probes.q: A patient has ptosis, a dilated pupil, and a 'down and out' eye. Which nerve is palsied?
probes.a: The IIIrd (oculomotor) nerve.

probes.q: Why does a compressive IIIrd nerve palsy involve the pupil while a diabetic (ischaemic) one usually spares it?
probes.a: The parasympathetic pupillary fibres run on the outer surface of the nerve; a compressive lesion from outside damages them early, while an ischaemic lesion affects the core of the nerve first and spares the peripheral pupillary fibres.

probes.q: A new IIIrd nerve palsy with a dilated, poorly reactive pupil. What must be urgently excluded?
probes.a: A compressive lesion, classically a posterior communicating artery aneurysm.

rubric.text: Tests eye movements in an H-shaped path and asks about diplopia
Explicitly comments on pupil involvement in any IIIrd nerve palsy
Tests both direct and consensual light reflex

skill.exam.neuro.cn5.title: CN V: the trigeminal nerve
skill.exam.neuro.cn5.oneLine: Sensation in three divisions, motor bulk and jaw deviation, then the corneal reflex and jaw jerk
skill.exam.neuro.cn5.why: The trigeminal nerve is both the sensory supply to almost the whole face and the motor supply to the muscles of chewing, so a complete exam has two quite different halves. The jaw jerk is one of the few reflexes that is exaggerated only by a BILATERAL upper motor neurone lesion, which makes it a specific bedside test for pseudobulbar palsy.

steps.text: Test light touch and pin-prick in each of the three divisions (ophthalmic, maxillary, mandibular), comparing side to side and comparing the perioral region to the rest of the face.
Assess the motor component: palpate the masseters bilaterally as the patient clenches the jaw, feeling for symmetrical bulk and contraction.
Ask the patient to open the jaw against resistance and watch for deviation.
Elicit the corneal reflex by lightly touching the upper cornea, from the side, with a wisp of cotton.
Elicit the jaw jerk: rest a finger across the middle of the chin with the mouth relaxed and slightly open, and tap the finger with the reflex hammer.

skill.exam.neuro.cn5.normal: Symmetrical sensation in all three divisions; symmetrical masseter bulk and contraction; jaw opens in the midline; brisk bilateral corneal blink; minimal or absent jaw jerk.
skill.exam.neuro.cn5.abnormal: Sensory loss in one or more divisions; unilateral masseter wasting or weakness; jaw deviating to one side on opening; an absent corneal reflex; an exaggerated jaw jerk.
skill.exam.neuro.cn5.significance: Unilateral motor weakness localises to the trigeminal motor root, ganglion or brainstem on that side. An exaggerated jaw jerk means bilateral corticobulbar (upper motor neurone) disease above the pons, as in pseudobulbar palsy or motor neurone disease; the corneal reflex tests the afferent limb of CN V against the efferent limb of CN VII, so an absent reflex can localise to either nerve depending on what else is found.

teach.heading: The jaw deviates TOWARD the weak side
teach.body: On opening the jaw, the unopposed action of the normal-side lateral pterygoid pushes the jaw across to the WEAK side. This is the 'pushing' half of the book's rule of 17 (the 12+5 rule): trigeminal and hypoglossal are both pushing muscles, so both deviate toward the affected side. The facial and vagus nerves, by contrast, are pulling muscles, and deviate the mouth or uvula toward the NORMAL side.
teach.note: Watching the midline notch between the upper and lower incisors as the jaw opens is the most reliable way to catch a subtle deviation.

teach.heading: Corneal reflex: read the pattern to localise
teach.body: Stimulate one eye at a time and watch BOTH eyes, then work out which limb, afferent (V) or efferent (VII), explains the pattern.
teach.note: Stimulating the AFFECTED eye tells you about the afferent (trigeminal) limb; watching the RESPONSE in each eye tells you about the efferent (facial) limb on that side.

teach.heading: The jaw jerk is specific for a bilateral upper motor neurone lesion
teach.body: A single, unilateral upper motor neurone lesion above the pons generally does NOT exaggerate the jaw jerk, because the trigeminal motor nucleus has bilateral corticobulbar input. A markedly brisk jaw jerk therefore points specifically to BILATERAL disease of the corticobulbar tracts, pseudobulbar palsy from bilateral strokes, or motor neurone disease being the classic examples.

teach.heading: Trigeminal neuralgia, for pattern recognition
teach.body: Brief, severe, electric-shock-like unilateral facial pain, usually in the maxillary or mandibular division, triggered by touching the face, chewing, or cold air, is the classic history of trigeminal neuralgia (tic douloureux). It is most often caused by a vascular loop compressing the nerve root; bilateral trigeminal neuralgia should raise multiple sclerosis.

pitfalls: Testing only touch and forgetting pain/temperature, missing a dissociated sensory loss.
Not watching the incisor midline carefully enough to catch a subtle jaw deviation.
Interpreting an absent corneal reflex without working out whether the afferent or efferent side is at fault.
Assuming a brisk jaw jerk in isolation is significant without checking for other bilateral upper motor neurone signs.

probes.q: On opening the jaw, it deviates to the left. Which side is weak?
probes.a: The left side (the jaw deviates toward the side of weakness).

probes.q: Touching the left cornea produces no blink in either eye, but touching the right cornea produces a blink in both eyes. Which limb of the reflex is affected, and on which side?
probes.a: The afferent (trigeminal, sensory) limb on the left, since stimulating the left eye gets no response anywhere, while stimulating the right eye still triggers a normal consensual response in the left eye.

probes.q: A markedly exaggerated jaw jerk. What does that specifically indicate?
probes.a: A bilateral lesion of the corticobulbar tracts above the trigeminal motor nucleus, as in pseudobulbar palsy or motor neurone disease, since a single unilateral upper motor neurone lesion does not exaggerate this reflex.

rubric.text: Tests all three divisions and compares both sides
Palpates masseter bulk and checks jaw deviation on opening
Elicits and correctly interprets the corneal reflex or jaw jerk

skill.exam.neuro.cn7.title: CN VII: the facial nerve
skill.exam.neuro.cn7.oneLine: The forehead-sparing test is the single most important thing this skill teaches
skill.exam.neuro.cn7.why: Whether the forehead is spared or not is what separates a peripheral (Bell's) palsy from a stroke at the bedside, before any scan. Getting this wrong in either direction, treating a stroke as Bell's palsy or the reverse, has real consequences.

steps.text: Inspect at rest for facial asymmetry, a flattened nasolabial fold, and the frequency and symmetry of spontaneous blinking.
Ask the patient to wrinkle the forehead/raise the eyebrows (frontalis, temporal branch).
Ask the patient to shut the eyes tightly while you try to prise them open (orbicularis oculi, zygomatic branch).
Ask the patient to show their teeth or smile, and to puff out both cheeks against your fingers (buccal branch).
If indicated, test taste on the anterior two-thirds of the protruded tongue, and comment on hyperacusis and lacrimation.

skill.exam.neuro.cn7.normal: Symmetrical spontaneous expression and blinking, symmetrical forehead wrinkling, both eyes close fully against resistance, symmetrical smile, and both cheeks resist deflation equally.
skill.exam.neuro.cn7.abnormal: Flattening of the nasolabial fold, weak or absent forehead wrinkling on one side, incomplete eye closure with the eyeball rolling up (Bell's phenomenon), a smile that pulls to the normal side, or air escaping from one puffed cheek.
skill.exam.neuro.cn7.significance: The forehead has BILATERAL cortical (upper motor neurone) representation, so a supranuclear (stroke) lesion spares it and only weakens the lower face; a lower motor neurone (Bell's palsy, or any lesion of the nerve itself) lesion weakens the WHOLE side, forehead included. Getting this distinction right at the bedside is one of the highest-yield tests in the whole cranial nerve exam.

teach.heading: Upper motor neurone versus lower motor neurone facial palsy

rows: Weak, opposite side to the lesion
Weak, same side as the lesion

teach.note: This works because the forehead's motor neurones receive corticobulbar input from BOTH hemispheres, so one-sided cortical damage cannot fully silence it; the lower face receives input mainly from the opposite hemisphere alone.

teach.heading: The rule of 10+7: which way the mouth deviates
teach.body: In a facial (or vagus) palsy, the muscles that pull the corner of the mouth (or the uvula) are weakened on the affected side, so the unopposed normal side PULLS the angle of the mouth, or the uvula, TOWARD ITSELF, the normal side. This is the opposite direction to a trigeminal or hypoglossal lesion, where the affected muscle PUSHES, and so the jaw or tongue deviates toward the weak side instead.

teach.heading: Where in the facial canal the lesion sits changes what else is lost

rows: Taste (anterior 2/3 tongue), salivary/lacrimal secretion, hyperacusis, plus possible VIII and V involvement, ipsilateral ataxia
Facial canal, above the chorda tympani
Taste and salivary secretion lost, hyperacusis present
Facial canal, below the chorda tympani (or after it exits, distal lesion)
Motor weakness only, taste and secretion unaffected

teach.note: Working out where taste and hyperacusis are also affected localises a peripheral facial palsy along the length of the facial canal, which a simple 'weak on one side' description cannot do.

pitfalls: Diagnosing 'facial nerve palsy' without testing the forehead separately, which is exactly the step that distinguishes a stroke from Bell's palsy.
Missing Bell's phenomenon (the eyeball rolling up on attempted, incomplete closure), a genuine sign of lower motor neurone weakness.
Confusing the direction of mouth deviation, since it is the opposite convention to the trigeminal/hypoglossal 'pushing' pattern.

probes.q: A patient cannot wrinkle either side of the forehead, and the whole left side of the face, including the forehead, is weak. UMN or LMN facial palsy?
probes.a: Lower motor neurone, because the forehead is involved.

probes.q: Why does the forehead escape weakness in a supranuclear (UMN) facial palsy but not in a Bell's palsy?
probes.a: The forehead's motor neurones get corticobulbar input from both cerebral hemispheres, so a one-sided cortical lesion cannot fully silence them; a lesion of the nerve itself (LMN) removes all input to that side, forehead included.

probes.q: A patient with a left LMN facial palsy also has hyperacusis and loss of taste on the anterior two-thirds of the tongue. Roughly where in the facial canal is the lesion?
probes.a: Proximal to the chorda tympani (above where it branches off), since both taste and the nerve to stapedius (which prevents hyperacusis) are affected.

rubric.text: Tests forehead wrinkling separately from the lower face
Checks for Bell's phenomenon on attempted eye closure
Correctly states whether the pattern is UMN or LMN

skill.exam.neuro.cn8.title: CN VIII: hearing and balance
skill.exam.neuro.cn8.oneLine: Rinne's and Weber's for hearing; a bedside screen for vestibular function
skill.exam.neuro.cn8.why: The two components of this nerve, cochlear and vestibular, fail in different diseases with different bedside tests. Rinne's and Weber's test together, rather than either alone, are what actually distinguish a conductive from a sensorineural hearing loss.

steps.text: Screen hearing gross by rubbing fingers near each ear, or whispering a number, comparing sides.
Rinne's test: strike a 512 Hz tuning fork, place it on the mastoid process until no longer heard, then move it beside the ear; ask which was louder or whether it is still audible beside the ear.
Weber's test: place the vibrating fork in the midline on the vertex, and ask where the sound is heard, in the midline or lateralised to one ear.
Screen vestibular function by asking about vertigo and observing for spontaneous or positional nystagmus.

skill.exam.neuro.cn8.normal: Air conduction heard louder/longer than bone conduction on each side (Rinne positive, bilaterally); Weber's heard equally in the midline; no nystagmus or vertigo.
skill.exam.neuro.cn8.abnormal: Bone conduction louder than air (Rinne negative); Weber's lateralising to one ear; nystagmus, especially triggered by a change in head position.
skill.exam.neuro.cn8.significance: Rinne's and Weber's together localise a hearing loss to conductive or sensorineural, and to which ear, without any equipment beyond a tuning fork. The pattern of nystagmus (fast component, whether it is suppressed by visual fixation, whether vertigo and hearing loss travel with it) separates a peripheral, usually benign, cause from a central one that needs urgent imaging.

teach.heading: Rinne's and Weber's, read together
teach.body: Neither test alone is conclusive; read the pair as one pattern.

rows: Negative (bone conduction louder than air, BC > AC)
Lateralises AWAY, to the normal ear

teach.note: A single test can mislead on its own, a mild conductive loss can still leave Rinne's 'positive'; always read both tests as one pattern, not in isolation.

teach.heading: Central versus peripheral vertigo, at the bedside
teach.note: The COWS mnemonic for caloric testing (Cold water gives nystagmus to the Opposite side, Warm gives nystagmus to the Same side) is used mainly in the unconscious patient; at the bedside in an awake patient, the pattern in the table above does most of the work.

teach.heading: The doll's-eye (oculocephalic) reflex tests far more than CN VIII
teach.body:
Turning the head passively while watching the eyes tests the vestibular apparatus, the brainstem vestibular nuclei, the medial longitudinal fasciculus, and CN III and VI together. An INTACT reflex in an unconscious patient (eyes stay fixed on a point in space as the head turns) means much of the brainstem is functioning, and argues for a non-structural cause of the coma; an ABSENT reflex suggests destructive brainstem pathology.

NEVER perform this on a patient with known or suspected cervical spine injury (trauma, an unclear collapse) until the C-spine is cleared: passive head-turning in an unstable neck risks cord injury. Confirm the neck is safe to move first.

pitfalls: Interpreting Rinne's alone without Weber's, which can miss a mild conductive loss.
Not asking specifically about associated tinnitus or hearing loss when assessing vertigo, which is what points toward a peripheral cause.
Missing that nystagmus suppressed by visual fixation favours a peripheral, not central, cause.

probes.q: In a conductive hearing loss, is Rinne's test positive or negative in the affected ear?
probes.a: Negative: bone conduction is heard louder than air conduction (BC > AC).

probes.q: Weber's test lateralises to the LEFT ear. Rinne's is positive (normal) on both sides. What kind of hearing loss, and in which ear?
probes.a: A sensorineural loss in the RIGHT ear, since Weber's lateralises away from a sensorineural deficit, toward the better (normal) ear.

probes.q: Give two features that favour a peripheral over a central cause of vertigo.
probes.a: Associated hearing loss/tinnitus, and nystagmus that is suppressed by visual fixation (also: acute/transient course, absence of other neurological signs).

rubric.text: Performs Rinne's test correctly on each side
Performs Weber's test and states the lateralisation
Screens for associated hearing loss/tinnitus when assessing vertigo

skill.exam.neuro.cn9_10.title: CN IX and X: the glossopharyngeal and vagus nerves
skill.exam.neuro.cn9_10.oneLine: Palate, gag and voice, examined together because these two nerves are almost inseparable at the bedside
skill.exam.neuro.cn9_10.why: The glossopharyngeal and vagus share so much overlapping supply, and leave the skull and travel through the neck together, that isolated CN IX dysfunction is rarely detectable on its own. In practice they are examined and interpreted as a pair.

steps.text: Listen to the voice for hoarseness or a nasal quality, and ask about any difficulty swallowing.
Ask the patient to say 'Ah' with the mouth open, and watch the soft palate rise symmetrically and the uvula stay midline.
Elicit the gag reflex by touching the posterior pharyngeal wall or tonsillar pillar on each side with a tongue depressor, watching for symmetrical elevation of the palate.
Assess swallowing directly if there is any suggestion of dysphagia.

skill.exam.neuro.cn9_10.normal: A clear voice, symmetrical palatal elevation with a midline uvula, and a brisk, symmetrical gag reflex bilaterally.
skill.exam.neuro.cn9_10.abnormal: A hoarse or nasal voice, palatal droop with the uvula pulled to one side, or an absent gag reflex on one side.
skill.exam.neuro.cn9_10.significance: The uvula deviates AWAY from the weak side (toward the normal side), the same 'pulling' pattern as the facial nerve. A unilaterally absent gag reflex is a genuine lower motor neurone sign; gag reflex can be physiologically absent bilaterally in some normal people, so a BILATERALLY absent gag is far less specific than a one-sided absence.

teach.heading: Uvula deviation follows the facial nerve's 'pulling' rule
teach.body: Palatopharyngeus, supplied by the vagus, pulls the uvula toward its own side when it contracts. A weak side cannot pull, so the unopposed normal side pulls the uvula TOWARD ITSELF, away from the lesion. This is the same convention as the facial nerve (the 10+7 half of the book's rule of 17), and the opposite convention to the trigeminal and hypoglossal nerves, which push the jaw or tongue toward the weak side instead.

teach.heading: The gag reflex: what it actually tests, and its limits
teach.body: The afferent limb is carried by CN IX, the efferent limb by CN IX and X together, with the reflex centre in the medulla. A UNILATERALLY absent gag is a genuine lower motor neurone finding. A bilaterally absent gag can be a normal variant in some healthy adults, so on its own it is far less useful; conversely, a HYPERACTIVE gag can occur with bilateral corticobulbar disease, as in pseudobulbar palsy.

teach.heading: Bulbar palsy versus pseudobulbar palsy
teach.note: Emotional lability is a genuinely useful bedside clue: it points to pseudobulbar palsy and a bilateral corticobulbar lesion, not to a lower motor neurone bulbar process.

teach.heading: Recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy, a vagal branch worth knowing separately
teach.body: A hoarse voice from a unilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy can come from mitral stenosis (left atrial enlargement), a bronchogenic carcinoma, an aortic aneurysm, or Hodgkin's disease compressing the nerve in the chest or neck; bilateral palsy, causing stridor, is seen after thyroid surgery or in Guillain-Barre syndrome.

pitfalls: Interpreting a bilaterally absent gag reflex as pathological, when it can be a normal variant.
Missing that the uvula deviates toward the NORMAL side, and reading the finding backward.
Not listening to the voice and asking about swallowing, both of which are simple, high-yield screens for vagal function.

probes.q: On saying 'Ah', the uvula pulls to the right. Which side is weak?
probes.a: The left side; the uvula deviates toward the normal (right) side, away from the weak side.

probes.q: Is a bilaterally absent gag reflex, on its own, a reliable sign of disease?
probes.a: No; it can be a normal finding in some healthy individuals. A UNILATERALLY absent gag is the more reliable, localising finding.

probes.q: A patient has a wasted, fasciculating tongue lying still in the mouth, and an absent gag reflex. Bulbar or pseudobulbar palsy?
probes.a: Bulbar palsy (a lower motor neurone process).

rubric.text: Watches palatal elevation and uvula position on phonation
Elicits the gag reflex and interprets a unilateral versus bilateral absence correctly
Comments on voice quality and asks about swallowing

skill.exam.neuro.cn11_12.title: CN XI and XII: accessory and hypoglossal nerves
skill.exam.neuro.cn11_12.oneLine: Shrug and turn for CN XI; protrude and push for CN XII
skill.exam.neuro.cn11_12.why: These are the two purely motor cranial nerves left to test, and both give a mechanically simple, high-yield sign: a shoulder that will not shrug, or a tongue that deviates on protrusion. Both also follow the trigeminal's 'pushing' convention rather than the facial nerve's 'pulling' one.

steps.text: CN XI, sternocleidomastoid: ask the patient to turn the head to one side against your resisting hand, then repeat for the other side, feeling and watching the opposite muscle contract.
CN XI, trapezius: ask the patient to shrug both shoulders against downward resistance, comparing the two sides.
CN XII: inspect the resting tongue in the mouth for wasting or fasciculations, then ask the patient to protrude it, watching for deviation.
Ask the patient to push the tongue against the inside of each cheek while you give counter-resistance from outside.

skill.exam.neuro.cn11_12.normal: Symmetrical, full-strength head turning and shoulder shrug; a tongue that protrudes in the midline with no wasting or fasciculation and pushes equally against both cheeks.
skill.exam.neuro.cn11_12.abnormal: Weak head turning or shoulder shrug on one side; a wasted or fasciculating tongue; tongue deviation on protrusion.
skill.exam.neuro.cn11_12.significance: For CN XI, weak turning of the head to the RIGHT tests the LEFT sternocleidomastoid (each SCM turns the head to the opposite side); a flat, non-contracting muscle on attempted turning localises the lesion. For CN XII, the tongue follows the trigeminal's 'pushing' convention: it deviates TOWARD the weak side on protrusion, because the normal-side genioglossus pushes it across.

teach.heading: Sternocleidomastoid turns the head to the OPPOSITE side
teach.body: Each SCM contracts to turn the head away from itself. So testing right head-turn against resistance is testing LEFT SCM strength, and a weak left SCM shows up as weakness turning the head to the right. Bilateral SCM weakness instead shows up as difficulty flexing the neck forward against resistance.

teach.heading: Trapezius, tested properly
teach.body: The traditional shoulder shrug against resistance also recruits levator scapulae, so it can under-detect a mild trapezius weakness. A more specific test resists the patient's attempt to bring the back of the head toward the acromion (for upper trapezius), or pushes the elbow forward while the arm is held out horizontally, palm up (for middle/lower trapezius). Weakness of the middle trapezius produces winging of the scapula.

teach.heading: Tongue deviation follows the 'pushing' rule, same as CN V
teach.body: The genioglossus PUSHES the tongue forward and to the opposite side. A weak genioglossus cannot push, so the tongue is pushed by the normal side instead and deviates TOWARD the weak side on protrusion. This is the second half of the book's rule of 17 ('12 + 5'): trigeminal and hypoglossal both push, and both deviate toward the affected side, the opposite convention to the facial and vagus nerves, which pull toward the normal side.

teach.heading: Reading the tongue on inspection alone

rows: Wasted, fasciculating, lying still, deviates on protrusion
Small and stiff, cannot be fully protruded, no fasciculations
Upper motor neurone (UMN) XII palsy (usually bilateral, as part of pseudobulbar palsy)

teach.note: Fasciculations at rest, with the tongue relaxed inside a slightly open mouth, are the single most specific finding for a lower motor neurone process (motor neurone disease being the classic worry).

pitfalls: Forgetting that testing right head-turn tests LEFT sternocleidomastoid, and reporting the side backward.
Using only the shoulder shrug to test trapezius, which under-detects mild weakness because levator scapulae compensates.
Missing fasciculations because the tongue was inspected while protruded and moving rather than resting still in the mouth.

probes.q: A patient is weak turning their head to the right. Which sternocleidomastoid is weak?
probes.a: The left sternocleidomastoid (each SCM turns the head to the opposite side).

probes.q: On protrusion, the tongue deviates to the right, with wasting and fasciculations on that side. UMN or LMN, and which side is weak?
probes.a: Lower motor neurone, and the RIGHT side is weak (the tongue deviates toward the weak side because the normal-side genioglossus pushes it across).

probes.q: Why is the traditional shoulder-shrug test an imperfect way to assess trapezius strength alone?
probes.a: Because levator scapulae also contributes to shoulder shrugging, so a mild isolated trapezius weakness can be masked; testing resisted head-to-acromion approximation or scapular winging is more specific.

rubric.text: Tests SCM correctly and states the contralateral relationship
Tests trapezius beyond the simple shrug when weakness is suspected
Inspects the resting tongue for fasciculations before asking for protrusion
