skill.exam.neuro.tone_power.title: Tone and power
skill.exam.neuro.tone_power.oneLine: Attitude and bulk first, then tone, then power against a fixed scale, and the drift tests for weakness too subtle to grade
skill.exam.neuro.tone_power.why: Tone tells you upper or lower motor neurone before you have finished testing power. Getting this pattern right is what separates a stroke from Guillain-Barre syndrome at the bedside, long before any scan; the drift tests then catch weakness too mild for the MRC scale to register at all.

steps.text: Note the resting attitude of the limbs: a flexed arm and extended, internally rotated leg at rest is the classic hemiplegic posture.
Inspect and, where needed, measure muscle bulk at fixed points from a bony landmark, comparing the two sides.

Assess tone by passively moving each joint through its range, asking the patient to relax; in the leg, roll the whole limb and watch the foot, or lift the knee suddenly and watch whether the heel drags.
Test power against a fixed scale (MRC 0 to 5) for each muscle group, comparing both sides, proximal and distal separately.
If power looks normal but a subtle lesion is suspected, test for pronator drift: arms out, palms up, eyes closed, held for 20 to 30 seconds.

skill.exam.neuro.tone_power.normal: Normal resting posture, no wasting, normal tone throughout, power 5/5 in all muscle groups symmetrically, no drift.
skill.exam.neuro.tone_power.abnormal: An abnormal resting attitude; wasting (more than 1 to 2 cm difference in circumference at a matched point); increased tone (spasticity or rigidity) or decreased tone (flaccidity); reduced power in any distribution; a positive pronator drift.
skill.exam.neuro.tone_power.significance: Increased tone with pyramidal-pattern weakness (extensors weaker than flexors in the arm, flexors weaker than extensors in the leg) means an upper motor neurone lesion. Flaccid tone with wasting and a focal or glove-and-stocking pattern means a lower motor neurone or peripheral problem. A positive drift with the eyes closed can mean either a motor or a sensory (posterior column) deficit, depending on exactly how the arm moves.

teach.heading: Upper motor neurone versus lower motor neurone, the whole pattern
teach.note: Learn this as ONE pattern, not five separate facts. A patient either fits the upper motor neurone row across the board or the lower motor neurone row; a mixed picture should make you reconsider the localisation.

teach.heading: Spasticity is not the same thing as rigidity

rows: Lead-pipe, or cog-wheel if tremor is superimposed
Worse with a fast passive movement

teach.note: Test the wrist by pronating/supinating the forearm and rolling the hand: a ratchet-like catch with tremor superimposed is cog-wheel rigidity, best felt with the other hand doing something else (like tapping) to bring it out.

teach.heading: Grade power on the MRC scale
points: 1: a flicker of contraction, no movement.
3: movement against gravity, not against resistance.
teach.note: Grade 4 is often subdivided (4-, 4, 4+) in practice, but do not blur 4 and 5. The difference between 'normal' and 'reduced' power matters clinically even when it is subtle.

teach.heading: Bulk: what actually counts as wasting, and where to look
teach.body: A circumference difference of more than about 1 cm on the dominant limb, or 2 cm on the non-dominant limb, at a fixed distance from a bony landmark, counts as true wasting rather than normal asymmetry. Some sites (thenar and hypothenar eminences, the shoulder) are usually assessed by inspection alone, since wasting there is often obvious without a tape measure.
teach.note: The 'split hand' sign, wasting of the first dorsal interosseous and hypothenar muscles with the thenar eminence relatively spared, is highly specific for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and does not fit any single nerve, root or plexus distribution.

teach.heading: Pronator drift and its relatives catch what grading alone misses
teach.body: With eyes closed and arms held out, palms up, a weak side slowly pronates and drifts down; this is the classic sign of a contralateral corticospinal lesion. What accompanies the drift changes its meaning.

points.d: A motor deficit.

points.t: Drift appears only once the eyes CLOSE.
points.d: A sensory (posterior column/proprioceptive) deficit, since visual feedback was compensating for it.
Cerebellar, not corticospinal.

points.t: The arm rises overhead without the patient noticing ('updrift').
points.d: A parietal lobe lesion with loss of position sense.

points.t: The arm drifts without any pronation.
points.d: Suggests a functional (non-organic) rather than structural cause.

pitfalls: Testing power without first assessing tone, and so missing the pattern that would have told you where to look.
Not comparing proximal with distal, which is what separates a myopathy from a neuropathy.
Grading power as 'normal' without actually testing against resistance.
Skipping the pronator drift in a patient with a normal formal power exam but a suggestive history, and missing a subtle hemiparesis.

probes.q: Spastic tone with an extensor plantar response. Upper or lower motor neurone?
probes.a: Upper motor neurone.

probes.q: Give the full lower motor neurone pattern: tone, bulk, reflexes, plantar.
probes.a: Reduced tone, wasting, reduced or absent reflexes, and a flexor or absent plantar response.

probes.q: Proximal weakness in both legs, normal reflexes, normal sensation. What category of disease?
probes.a: Likely a myopathy, since proximal, symmetrical weakness with preserved reflexes and sensation is the classic myopathic pattern, unlike the distal pattern typical of most peripheral neuropathies.

probes.q: A patient's outstretched arm drifts down only after their eyes are closed, not while their eyes are open. What does this suggest?
probes.a: A sensory (posterior column/proprioceptive) deficit rather than a pure motor one, since vision was compensating for the loss of position sense until it was removed.

rubric.text: Assesses tone before testing power
Grades power against the MRC scale
Compares proximal with distal and both sides
Tests for pronator drift when a subtle deficit is suspected

skill.exam.neuro.reflexes.title: Deep tendon reflexes, superficial reflexes and the plantar response
skill.exam.neuro.reflexes.oneLine: A reflex arc has two ends; knowing which end is broken localises the lesion, and clonus tells you how far it's broken
skill.exam.neuro.reflexes.why: A reflex is a simple arc: sensory afferent, spinal segment, motor efferent. An absent or exaggerated reflex tells you which part of that arc, and therefore which level of the nervous system, has failed. Superficial reflexes and clonus extend the same logic beyond the deep tendon reflexes alone.

steps.text: Ensure the limb is relaxed and positioned correctly for each reflex.
Strike the tendon briskly with the reflex hammer, letting the hammer fall under its own weight.
Compare both sides for every reflex tested, and grade each on a 0 to 4+ scale.
If a reflex is absent, reinforce with a distraction manoeuvre (Jendrassik) and try again before calling it truly absent.
Elicit the superficial abdominal and cremasteric reflexes by stroking, not tapping.
Test the plantar response, stroking the lateral sole firmly with a blunt object, and if the reflexes above it are brisk, check for ankle clonus.

skill.exam.neuro.reflexes.normal: Symmetrical, grade 2+ reflexes, present superficial reflexes, a flexor (downgoing) plantar response, no clonus.
skill.exam.neuro.reflexes.abnormal: Exaggerated, reduced, absent, or asymmetrical deep tendon reflexes; absent superficial reflexes; an extensor (upgoing) plantar response; sustained clonus.
skill.exam.neuro.reflexes.significance: Exaggerated reflexes with an extensor plantar and absent superficial reflexes together mean an upper motor neurone (pyramidal) lesion above the level tested. Absent deep tendon reflexes mean a lesion of the reflex arc itself, at the nerve, root, or spinal segment level. Sustained clonus is simply a more marked form of hyperreflexia and carries the same significance as a very brisk reflex.

teach.heading: The segments, so you can localise
teach.note: A reflex that is absent at one specific level with normal reflexes above and below points precisely at that segment, which is exactly how a single nerve root lesion is localised. Mnemonic, reading bottom to top: S1,2 : L3,4 : C5,6 : C7,8.

teach.heading: Grade every reflex on the same 0 to 4+ scale

rows: Markedly hyperactive, pathological, often with clonus

teach.heading: Superficial reflexes work the opposite way to deep tendon reflexes

rows: Stroke the abdominal wall toward the umbilicus
Stroke the upper inner thigh; testis rises

teach.note: Superficial reflexes are ABOLISHED by a pyramidal tract lesion, the opposite of what happens to deep tendon reflexes. An absent abdominal reflex, with brisk knee and ankle jerks, fits the same upper motor neurone picture as an extensor plantar.

teach.heading: Clonus: how to elicit it, and what it means
teach.body: Ankle clonus is elicited by supporting the knee, then briskly dorsiflexing the foot and holding gentle pressure on the sole. A few beats that fade are unsustained clonus; rhythmic beats that continue as long as the pressure is held are sustained clonus, a pathological finding equivalent to a very brisk (4+) reflex.
teach.note: A few beats of unsustained clonus can occur in anxious, otherwise normal individuals, and in hyperthyroidism; SUSTAINED clonus is what should be treated as pathological.

teach.heading: Reading the plantar response correctly
teach.body: Stroke firmly along the lateral border of the sole from heel to the base of the little toe, then curving medially. A normal response is flexion (downgoing) of the great toe. Extension (upgoing), with or without fanning of the other toes, is the Babinski sign.
teach.note: The Babinski sign is present from birth until about 18 months, when the corticospinal tracts myelinate; an extensor response beyond that age is always abnormal and means an upper motor neurone lesion somewhere between the cortex and the spinal segment tested. If direct plantar stimulation is equivocal, Chaddock's method (stroking below the lateral malleolus) is the most useful alternative technique.

pitfalls: Striking too gently, or not letting the hammer fall freely.
Not reinforcing before calling a reflex truly absent.
Confusing withdrawal from a ticklish sole with a genuine plantar response.
Recording a few beats of unsustained clonus as pathological, when only sustained clonus reliably is.
Forgetting to test the superficial abdominal reflexes, which carry the same localising weight as the plantar response.

probes.q: Which segments does the ankle reflex test?
probes.a: S1 and S2.

probes.q: What is the Babinski sign, and what does it mean in an adult?
probes.a: Extension (upgoing) of the great toe on plantar stimulation, with or without fanning of the other toes. In an adult it always indicates an upper motor neurone lesion.

probes.q: A patient has an absent knee reflex on one side but a normal ankle reflex on the same side. What does that pattern suggest?
probes.a: A lesion affecting specifically the L3/L4 segment or its root on that side, since the reflex arc immediately above and below is intact.

probes.q: Absent abdominal reflexes plus brisk knee and ankle jerks and an extensor plantar. What single process explains all three findings together?
probes.a: An upper motor neurone (pyramidal) lesion: it abolishes superficial reflexes while exaggerating deep tendon reflexes and producing an extensor plantar, all from the same loss of descending inhibition.

rubric.text: Uses correct hammer technique, letting it fall freely
Compares both sides for every reflex
Reinforces before calling a reflex absent
Tests at least one superficial reflex alongside the deep tendon reflexes

skill.exam.neuro.sensory.title: Sensory system examination
skill.exam.neuro.sensory.oneLine: Two separate pathways, tested with two separate sets of tools, and a pattern of loss that names the lesion
skill.exam.neuro.sensory.why: Pain and temperature travel by one spinal pathway, and touch, vibration and joint position by another, so testing only one of them can miss a lesion that spares the other completely. The PATTERN of what is lost, a single limb, a stocking distribution, or one side of the body below a level, is often more useful than any single finding.

steps.text: With the patient's eyes closed, test pin-prick (pain) over each dermatome, comparing side to side and asking whether it feels normal, reduced, or increased.
Test temperature with a cold and a warm object if pain sensation is abnormal, or if leprosy or a cord lesion is suspected.
Test light touch with a wisp of cotton, again with the eyes closed.
Test joint position sense at the most distal joint first (great toe metatarsophalangeal, finger distal interphalangeal); move it up or down and ask the patient to name the direction.
Test vibration with a 128 Hz tuning fork at the most distal bony point first, asking the patient to report when it stops; move proximally only if it is impaired distally.
If primary sensation is intact bilaterally, test cortical sensation: two-point discrimination, graphesthesia (tracing a number on the palm), and stereognosis (identifying an object by touch).
Perform Romberg's test: feet together, arms at the sides, first with eyes open, then closed, watching for swaying or falling.

skill.exam.neuro.sensory.normal: Symmetrical pain, temperature and touch throughout; joint position and vibration detected accurately at the most distal joint tested; intact two-point discrimination, graphesthesia and stereognosis; minimal sway on Romberg's with eyes open or closed.
skill.exam.neuro.sensory.abnormal: Any asymmetry or loss of a primary modality; impaired joint position or vibration sense; loss of a cortical sensation despite normal primary sensation; a positive Romberg's sign (gross swaying or falling once the eyes close).
skill.exam.neuro.sensory.significance: WHICH modalities are lost, and in what distribution, distinguishes a peripheral neuropathy (distal, symmetrical, glove-and-stocking, all modalities) from a cord lesion (a sensory level, often with dissociated loss) from a single nerve or root lesion (a defined patch matching that nerve or dermatome). Loss of cortical sensation with normal primary sensation localises specifically to the parietal lobe.

teach.heading: Two pathways, tested with two different toolkits

rows: Spinothalamic tract, crosses near the level it enters
Posterior columns (gracile/cuneate), crosses in the medulla
Cotton wisp, 128 Hz tuning fork, joint movement

teach.note: Because these two pathways cross at different levels, a single cord lesion can produce DISSOCIATED sensory loss, pain and temperature lost on one side with touch and proprioception lost on the other, which is exactly the pattern seen in Brown-Sequard syndrome and in the lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome.

teach.heading: Primary sensation intact, cortical sensation lost, means one thing
teach.body: Two-point discrimination, graphesthesia, stereognosis and tactile localisation all require an intact PARIETAL LOBE to integrate a normally-transmitted signal. If pin-prick, touch and vibration are all normal but the patient cannot identify a coin by feel or a number traced on their palm, the lesion is cortical (contralateral parietal), not peripheral.

teach.heading: Reading the pattern, not just the finding

rows: A defined patch matching one nerve or one dermatome
A single peripheral nerve or nerve root lesion
A clear level on the trunk, below which everything is lost, or dissociated (pain/temp one side, touch/proprioception the other)
Loss over one whole side of the face and body, sparing the trunk midline
A lesion above the brainstem (thalamus or cortex)

teach.note: On the trunk, TRUE organic sensory loss typically stops just short of the midline because of overlap from the opposite side; loss that crosses the midline exactly should raise a non-organic cause. This rule does not hold on the face, where there is less midline overlap, so organic facial sensory loss can genuinely reach the midline.

teach.heading: Vibration: the timed test is the most sensitive version
teach.body: Strike the tuning fork and place it over the most distal bony point (the great toe, then the medial malleolus if abnormal there). Time how long the patient reports feeling it. Normal is roughly 10 seconds or more in the lower limb and 20 seconds or more in the upper limb; a shorter duration than that is an early, sensitive sign of posterior column dysfunction, well before vibration is lost outright.
teach.note: 128 Hz is preferred for routine bedside testing because it decays slowly enough to time properly; 256 Hz decays faster and can pick up very early loss, as in subacute combined degeneration of the cord.

teach.heading: Romberg's sign is specifically a posterior column (proprioceptive) test
teach.body:
Balance while standing needs at least two of three inputs: vision, proprioception, and an intact cerebellum. Romberg's isolates proprioception by removing vision: if the patient is steady with eyes open but sways or falls once the eyes close, the cerebellum is presumed intact and the deficit is sensory (posterior column or peripheral large-fibre).

A patient who cannot stand steady even with eyes OPEN has a cerebellar or vestibular problem, not a Romberg-positive sensory one, and the test does not apply.

pitfalls: Testing touch alone and skipping pain and temperature, missing a dissociated sensory loss.
Moving proximally to test vibration and joint position without first establishing that the distal joint is actually normal.
Testing cortical sensation (stereognosis, graphesthesia) in a patient whose primary sensation is already abnormal, which makes the result impossible to interpret.
Calling Romberg's test positive in a patient who was already unsteady with their eyes open, when the sign specifically requires a change between eyes open and eyes closed.

probes.q: Which sensory pathway carries pain and temperature, and where does it cross?
probes.a: The spinothalamic tract, which crosses near the spinal level it enters (via the anterior white commissure).

probes.q: A patient has normal pin-prick, touch and vibration, but cannot identify a key placed in their hand with eyes closed, using either hand. What does this localise to?
probes.a: Bilateral parietal lobe dysfunction (a lesion affecting cortical/secondary sensory processing), since primary sensation is intact but stereognosis, a cortical sensation, is lost.

probes.q: A patient loses pain and temperature on the right side of the body below the umbilicus, and loses joint position and vibration on the left side below the same level. What syndrome is this, and why does it look this way?
probes.a: Brown-Sequard syndrome (cord hemisection): the spinothalamic tract has already crossed before ascending, so its loss appears on the side OPPOSITE the lesion, while the posterior columns have not yet crossed, so their loss appears on the SAME side as the lesion.

probes.q: A patient sways noticeably even with their eyes open, and this does not change much when their eyes close. Is this a positive Romberg's sign?
probes.a: No. Romberg's specifically tests the CHANGE between eyes open and eyes closed; a patient unsteady even with eyes open likely has a cerebellar or vestibular problem, and the test does not meaningfully apply.

rubric.text: Tests pain/temperature and touch/vibration/proprioception as two distinct systems
Starts testing vibration and joint position at the most distal joint
Describes the pattern of any loss, not just its presence
Performs Romberg's correctly, comparing eyes open to eyes closed

sources.locator: Approach to the patient with sensory loss

skill.exam.neuro.cerebellar.title: Cerebellar signs and coordination
skill.exam.neuro.cerebellar.oneLine: DANISH, one test per letter, plus the Romberg comparison that tells cerebellar apart from sensory ataxia
skill.exam.neuro.cerebellar.why: The cerebellum does not move anything itself; it times and scales movement that other systems generate, so its damage shows up as clumsiness and mistiming rather than weakness. A cerebellar lesion on one side produces signs on the SAME (ipsilateral) side of the body, unlike almost every other part of the motor system.

steps.text: Finger-nose test: ask the patient to touch their nose, then your finger held at arm's length, repeatedly and as accurately as possible; move your finger to vary the target.
Heel-shin test: with the patient supine, ask them to place one heel on the opposite knee and slide it smoothly down the shin to the ankle and back.
Dysdiadochokinesia: ask the patient to rapidly and repeatedly pronate and supinate the forearm, slapping one palm then the back of the hand on the other palm.
Rebound (Stewart-Holmes) test: have the patient pull against your resistance, then suddenly release it, protecting them from striking themselves.
Ask the patient to say a multisyllabic word (e.g. 'British constitution') and listen for scanning speech.
Observe for nystagmus at the extremes of gaze, and perform Romberg's test, comparing sway with eyes open and closed.

skill.exam.neuro.cerebellar.normal: Smooth, accurate finger-nose and heel-shin movements with no tremor; rapid, regular alternating movements; a normal rebound check; clear, evenly-paced speech; no nystagmus; minimal sway on Romberg's, unchanged between eyes open and closed.
skill.exam.neuro.cerebellar.abnormal: Past-pointing or an intention tremor worsening as the target is approached; a jerky, wavering heel-shin trace; slow, irregular, or clumsy alternating movements (dysdiadochokinesia); absent rebound check, with the limb continuing to move; scanning or staccato speech; nystagmus; a broad-based, unsteady gait that is NOT made worse by closing the eyes.
skill.exam.neuro.cerebellar.significance: These signs localise to the SAME side as the lesion in a cerebellar hemisphere. Truncal instability without limb ataxia points to the vermis (midline), while limb dysmetria and dysdiadochokinesia point to a hemisphere. Crucially, cerebellar ataxia is not made materially worse by closing the eyes, which is what separates it from a sensory ataxia at the bedside.

teach.heading: DANISH: one letter, one test

rows: Wide-based, reeling gait; jerky finger-nose or heel-shin
Fast component toward the side of the lesion
Tremor that worsens as the target is approached
Reduced resistance to passive movement, pendular knee jerk

teach.heading: Cerebellar signs are IPSILATERAL to the lesion
teach.body: This is the exception to remember: almost everything else in the motor exam (power, tone abnormalities from a corticospinal lesion) localises to the OPPOSITE side of a cerebral lesion, but a cerebellar hemisphere lesion produces incoordination on the SAME side, because the major cerebellar outflow pathways cross twice on their way to and from the cerebral cortex.

teach.heading: Rebound tests something dysmetria alone does not
teach.body: Have the patient pull hard against your resistance, then let go suddenly; normally the antagonist muscles check the movement almost immediately. In a SPASTIC limb, an exaggerated rebound is seen. In CEREBELLAR disease, this checking response is essentially absent, and the limb keeps moving in the original direction, sometimes striking the patient, which is why you protect them during the test.

teach.heading: Cerebellar ataxia versus sensory ataxia: the Romberg comparison decides it

rows: Wide, unsteady even with eyes open
Normal-to-wide, but relatively steadier with eyes open
Reasonably accurate if slow and visually guided; worse eyes closed

teach.note: This distinction matters because it points to two completely different differentials, cerebellum/brainstem versus a peripheral neuropathy or posterior column lesion, using only a bedside test that takes seconds.

teach.heading: Where the lesion sits changes the pattern

points.d: Truncal ataxia and gait instability, with little or no limb incoordination; often little dysarthria or nystagmus.
Ipsilateral limb dysmetria and dysdiadochokinesia, most noticeable in fine finger movements and speech.
All of the above together, bilaterally; seen with toxic-metabolic causes, paraneoplastic disease, or diffuse infectious/inflammatory processes.

pitfalls: Localising a cerebellar sign to the opposite side out of habit, forgetting it is ipsilateral.
Not comparing Romberg's with eyes open to eyes closed properly, which is what actually separates cerebellar from sensory ataxia.
Testing heel-shin with the patient sitting rather than supine, which lets gravity assist the movement and can mask mild dysmetria.
Failing to protect the patient during the rebound test.

probes.q: Expand the DANISH mnemonic for cerebellar signs.
probes.a: Dysdiadochokinesia, Ataxia, Nystagmus, Intention tremor, Scanning speech, Hypotonia.

probes.q: A left cerebellar hemisphere lesion. Which side shows the limb incoordination?
probes.a: The left side (cerebellar signs are ipsilateral to the lesion).

probes.q: A patient sways on Romberg's testing with their eyes open, and it is not much worse with the eyes closed. Cerebellar or sensory ataxia?
probes.a: Cerebellar ataxia; cerebellar disease is not materially worsened by removing visual input, unlike sensory (posterior column) ataxia.

probes.q: What does an absent rebound check, with the limb continuing to move after sudden release of resistance, indicate, and why must you protect the patient during this test?
probes.a: It indicates cerebellar disease, since the normal, near-immediate antagonist checking response is lost; the limb can continue moving unchecked and strike the patient, so the examiner must guard against this before releasing.

rubric.text: Performs finger-nose and heel-shin tests correctly
Correctly states cerebellar findings are ipsilateral to the lesion
Uses the eyes-open/eyes-closed Romberg comparison to distinguish cerebellar from sensory ataxia

skill.exam.neuro.gait.title: Gait examination
skill.exam.neuro.gait.oneLine: Watch first, name the pattern second: gait can localise a lesion faster than the rest of the exam combined
skill.exam.neuro.gait.why: Gait is a whole-system test that recruits motor, sensory, cerebellar and extrapyramidal function together, so an experienced observer can often localise a lesion within seconds of watching a patient walk, before any formal testing begins.

steps.text: Watch the patient rise from a chair without using their hands, if possible.
Observe walking away from you, then toward you, over several metres: posture, arm swing, step length and height, base width, and the ease of turning.
Ask the patient to walk heel-to-toe in a straight line (tandem gait).
Ask the patient to walk on their heels, then on their toes.
If a proprioceptive problem is suspected, repeat plain walking with the eyes closed only once safety can be assured, or rely on the seated Romberg's test instead.

skill.exam.neuro.gait.normal: Rises without using the hands; walks with a normal base, full-length stride, symmetrical arm swing, and turns easily; tandem gait is steady; heel and toe walking are both possible.
skill.exam.neuro.gait.abnormal: Needing the hands to rise; an asymmetrical, circumducted, shuffling, broad-based, waddling, or high-stepping gait; unsteady or impossible tandem walking; inability to walk on heels (foot drop) or toes (calf weakness).
skill.exam.neuro.gait.significance: Each named gait pattern maps to a specific level of the nervous system, so correctly naming the pattern is itself a working localisation, hemiparesis, peripheral nerve palsy, myopathy, cerebellar disease, posterior column loss, and basal ganglia disease each produce a gait that looks nothing like the others.

teach.heading: The named gaits, and what each one means
teach.body: Watch first, then match what you saw to one row below.

rows: The affected leg swings outward in an arc, extended and stiff; the arm is flexed and adducted
Both legs stiffly dragged, extended, sometimes crossing
Bilateral upper motor neurone lesion, e.g. cord compression, cerebral palsy
The foot slaps down; the knee is lifted higher to clear the floor
Lower motor neurone lesion, e.g. common peroneal nerve palsy, L5 radiculopathy
A broad-based, rolling gait, exaggerated lumbar lordosis, difficulty rising from sitting
Proximal muscle weakness, e.g. myopathy, muscular dystrophy
Reeling, unsteady, wide base, worse turning, veers toward the affected side
Broad-based, high-stepping, watches the feet, much worse with eyes closed or in the dark
Posterior column loss (B12 deficiency, tabes dorsalis) or large-fibre neuropathy
Stooped, small rapid steps, reduced arm swing, difficulty starting and stopping, may freeze
Feet appear 'stuck to the floor'; power, sensation and cerebellar function are all normal on the bed
Bilateral frontal lobe disease, normal pressure hydrocephalus

teach.note: In hemiparesis the asymmetry is obvious; in bilateral (paraparetic) disease both legs are affected together and the asymmetry can be subtle, so compare the two sides carefully rather than looking for one abnormal leg.

teach.heading: The eyes-open/eyes-closed rule works for gait too
teach.body: A sensory (posterior column) ataxic gait is dramatically worse with the eyes closed or in poor light, because the patient has been compensating for lost proprioception with vision; a cerebellar ataxic gait is not materially changed by removing vision, since the deficit is not a sensory one. This is the same logic as Romberg's test, applied to walking instead of standing still.

teach.heading: Tandem gait is a more sensitive screen than plain walking
teach.body: Walking heel-to-toe narrows the base of support and removes the small margin for error that ordinary walking allows, so it can reveal a mild cerebellar or sensory ataxia that looks unremarkable during normal gait.

teach.heading: A limp is not always neurological
teach.body: An antalgic (painful) gait, a shortened stance phase on the painful side, has an orthopaedic or rheumatological cause, not a neurological one, and should be distinguished from the gait patterns above before reaching for a neurological explanation.

pitfalls: Only watching the patient walk away, and missing an arm swing asymmetry that is more visible walking toward you.
Not distinguishing a painful (antalgic) limp from a genuine neurological gait disorder.
Skipping tandem gait, missing a mild ataxia that plain walking does not reveal.
Assuming a broad-based gait is always cerebellar without checking whether it is much worse with the eyes closed, which would instead point to a sensory cause.

probes.q: A patient's leg swings outward in an arc while walking, with the arm flexed against the chest on the same side. What is this gait called, and what does it suggest?
probes.a: A hemiplegic (circumduction) gait, suggesting an upper motor neurone lesion such as a stroke.

probes.q: A gait is broad-based and high-stepping, and becomes markedly worse when the patient's eyes are closed or the room is dark. What type of gait is this?
probes.a: A sensory ataxic (stamping) gait, from loss of proprioception (posterior column or large-fibre neuropathy).

probes.q: Why does tandem gait reveal a mild ataxia that ordinary walking can miss?
probes.a: Walking heel-to-toe narrows the base of support and removes the margin for error that a normal walking base allows, making mild incoordination visible.

rubric.text: Observes gait from both approaching and departing, and turning
Tests tandem gait
Correctly names the gait pattern and its likely level of lesion

skill.exam.neuro.meningeal.title: Meningeal signs
skill.exam.neuro.meningeal.oneLine: Neck stiffness, Kernig's, Brudzinski's and the tripod sign, all read as one set
skill.exam.neuro.meningeal.why: These signs exist because inflamed meninges hurt when they are stretched, so the body reflexively resists any movement that would stretch them. None is perfectly sensitive alone, which is exactly why they are elicited together rather than any one being relied on in isolation.

steps.text: Before any neck flexion: confirm there is no history or suspicion of cervical spine trauma. Do not attempt these manoeuvres on a patient with a possibly unstable neck until it has been cleared.
With the patient supine, gently attempt to flex the neck, bringing the chin toward the chest, and note any resistance or pain.
For Kernig's sign: flex the hip and knee to a right angle, then slowly extend the knee, watching for resistance or pain before full extension.
For Brudzinski's neck sign: with one hand behind the head and the other on the chest to stop the trunk rising, passively flex the neck and watch the hips and knees for reflex flexion.
Ask the patient to sit up unaided from lying flat, and watch how they do it (the tripod/Amoss sign).

skill.exam.neuro.meningeal.normal: The neck flexes freely with no pain; the knee extends fully past 135 degrees without resistance; no reflex hip/knee flexion on neck flexion; the patient sits up without needing to support themselves behind on extended arms.
skill.exam.neuro.meningeal.abnormal: Nuchal rigidity, with resistance and pain on neck flexion; a positive Kernig's sign, resistance or pain extending the knee before full extension; a positive Brudzinski's sign, reflex flexion of the hips and knees on neck flexion; a positive tripod sign, the patient propping themselves up behind with both arms to sit up.
skill.exam.neuro.meningeal.significance: Meningeal signs together suggest meningeal irritation, most importantly meningitis or subarachnoid haemorrhage, both of which need urgent evaluation. No single sign is sensitive enough to exclude meningitis on its own; a clinically convincing history should still prompt further workup even if these signs are negative, especially early in the illness or in an immunocompromised or very young or elderly patient.

teach.heading: Why these signs exist at all
teach.body: Inflammation of the meninges makes any manoeuvre that stretches them, flexing the neck, straightening a flexed hip's knee, painful, and the paravertebral and hamstring muscles reflexively resist that stretch. Nuchal rigidity classically shows a patient lying curled on their side, head extended, resisting any attempt at neck flexion, while rotation of the neck is relatively preserved and less painful.

teach.heading: Kernig's sign, precisely
teach.body: With the hip already flexed to a right angle, slowly extend the knee. A positive sign is resistance or pain that appears BEFORE the knee reaches full extension (classically before about 135 degrees), from stretch transmitted to the inflamed meninges via the sciatic nerve roots and hamstrings.

teach.heading: Brudzinski described four signs, but the neck sign is the one routinely tested

rows: Passive neck flexion, supine, trunk held down
Reflex flexion of both hips and knees
Reflex flexion of the OPPOSITE leg
Pressure on both cheeks below the zygoma
Reflex hip/knee flexion and leg abduction

teach.note: Only the neck sign is part of routine bedside screening; the other three are less commonly elicited but are worth recognising by name.

teach.heading: The tripod (Amoss) sign
teach.body: Sitting up from lying flat normally needs active neck flexion. A patient with meningeal irritation avoids that flexion by pushing themselves up with both arms placed far behind them on the bed, like a tripod, to take the load off the spine. In severe irritation this can progress to a fully arched, opisthotonic posture with the neck extended and the arms braced behind the pelvis.

teach.heading: Meningism is not the same as meningitis
teach.body:
'Meningism' describes the clinical PICTURE of neck stiffness and headache without necessarily meaning infective or haemorrhagic meningeal inflammation.

Cervical spondylosis, Parkinson's disease, raised intracranial pressure with impending tonsillar herniation, tetanus, and strychnine poisoning can all produce resistance to neck movement that mimics true meningeal irritation, so the whole clinical picture, fever, photophobia, rash, and CSF findings, still decides the diagnosis.

pitfalls: Flexing the neck for nuchal rigidity, Kernig's, or Brudzinski's in a patient with unexcluded cervical spine trauma - confirm the neck is safe to move first.
Relying on a single sign, most often neck stiffness alone, and stopping the exam there.
Missing that rotation of the neck can be relatively preserved in meningeal irritation even when flexion is markedly resisted.
Assuming all resistance to neck flexion is meningitis without considering cervical spondylosis, parkinsonism, or raised ICP with herniation risk.
Not escalating a clinically convincing history when the bedside signs are negative, since none of them is sensitive enough to exclude meningitis on its own.

probes.q: Describe how Kernig's sign is elicited and what a positive result looks like.
probes.a: With the hip flexed to a right angle, the knee is slowly extended; resistance or pain appearing before full extension (roughly before 135 degrees) is a positive sign.

probes.q: What is the tripod (Amoss) sign?
probes.a: When asked to sit up from lying flat, a patient with meningeal irritation avoids neck flexion by supporting themselves with both arms placed far behind them on the bed, like a tripod.

probes.q: A patient has clear clinical features suggesting meningitis, but Kernig's and Brudzinski's signs are both negative. Does this exclude meningitis?
probes.a: No; none of the meningeal signs is sensitive enough on its own to exclude meningitis, and a convincing clinical picture should still prompt further workup (lumbar puncture, imaging as indicated) regardless of a negative bedside exam.

rubric.text: Assesses neck flexion for nuchal rigidity
Correctly performs Kernig's sign
Interprets the signs together rather than relying on one alone

skill.hx.stroke.risk.title: The vascular risk history
skill.hx.stroke.risk.oneLine: The questions that explain WHY this happened, and that a preceding TIA is a missed warning, not a footnote
skill.hx.stroke.risk.why: The presenting complaint tells you a stroke happened; the risk history tells you why, and it is what secondary prevention is actually built on. A preceding TIA, in particular, is commonly under-reported by patients as 'nothing', because it resolved, and it is the single most important thing to ask about directly.

asks.text: Do you have high blood pressure, for how long, and do you take your tablets regularly?
Do you have diabetes, and how well controlled has it been?
Have you ever noticed a palpitation, a fluttering, or an irregular heartbeat?
Have you ever had a similar weakness, numbness, or a visual or speech problem before that got completely better on its own, even if it only lasted minutes?
Do you smoke, and has anyone checked your cholesterol?
Is anyone in your family known to have had a stroke or a heart attack at a young age?
What medicines do you take regularly, particularly anything that thins the blood, and in a woman of childbearing age, are you on an oral contraceptive?

teach.heading: A prior TIA is a rehearsal, not a reassurance
teach.body: Patients very often do not volunteer a resolved episode because it went away and they assumed it was nothing, cramp, tiredness, a trapped nerve. Ask about it directly and specifically, because the short-term risk of a completed stroke after a TIA is genuinely high, and finding one changes how urgently the current presentation, and any future warning sign, should be treated.

teach.heading: Why atrial fibrillation is asked about separately from 'any heart problems'
teach.body: A vague question about heart disease is easy for a patient to answer 'no' to if they have never been formally diagnosed with anything, even if they have felt an irregular heartbeat for years. Ask specifically about a fluttering or irregular sensation, because unrecognised atrial fibrillation is a common and correctable cause of cardioembolic stroke.

pitfalls: Accepting 'no heart problems' without asking specifically about palpitations or a known irregular pulse.
Not asking directly about a prior transient episode, and so missing a preceding TIA that the patient dismissed as unimportant.
Recording 'hypertensive' without asking about actual adherence, which is often the real, modifiable problem.

probes.q: Name four vascular risk factors to ask about in a suspected stroke.
probes.a: Hypertension, diabetes, atrial fibrillation/palpitations, smoking, dyslipidaemia, and a prior TIA or stroke.

probes.q: Why ask specifically about a resolved episode of weakness in the past, rather than just 'any past neurological problems'?
probes.a: Patients commonly dismiss a resolved episode as unimportant because it went away; a specific question uncovers a prior TIA, which carries a real short-term risk of a completed stroke and should already have prompted urgent evaluation.

rubric.text: Covers hypertension, diabetes, cardiac rhythm and a prior transient episode
Specifically asks about a prior resolved episode of neurological symptoms

skill.hx.cord.sphincter.title: Asking about the sensory level and the sphincters
skill.hx.cord.sphincter.oneLine: The questions patients least often volunteer, and most need to be asked directly
skill.hx.cord.sphincter.why: A band-like sensory change and a bladder or bowel symptom are both things patients frequently do not mention unless asked directly, either from embarrassment or because they had not connected them to their legs. Both are core parts of the compressive-myelopathy triad and change the urgency of the case.

asks.text: Is there any tight, band-like, or belt-like feeling anywhere around your chest or abdomen?
Did the weakness start in your feet and climb upward, or start in your hands and spread downward?
Have you had any difficulty starting or controlling your urine, or any accidental leaking?
Have you noticed any change in your bowel habit, constipation or loss of control?
Any back pain, and if so, is it worse lying flat or at night?
Any recent fever, night sweats or weight loss, and any known contact with tuberculosis?

teach.heading: Why the band sensation is worth asking about specifically
teach.body: A tight or constricting feeling at the level of the lesion, sometimes called a girdle or funicular sensation, can be the earliest sensory clue to where the compression is, often before a clear level is found on formal testing. It is easily mistaken by the patient for a digestive or cardiac symptom and is rarely offered without a direct question.

teach.heading: Sphincter symptoms are a red flag, not a footnote
teach.body: Urinary retention (often first noticed as hesitancy or straining, sometimes progressing to painless overflow), loss of bladder sensation, or new bowel incontinence or severe constipation all indicate that the lesion has already involved the autonomic pathways. Their presence changes this from an urgent case to an emergency one, because sphincter recovery is one of the outcomes most sensitive to how quickly decompression happens.

pitfalls: Not asking about bladder and bowel function directly, and relying on the patient to volunteer it.
Treating night-worse back pain as mechanical or musculoskeletal without asking about constitutional symptoms.
Missing the ascending-versus-descending pattern, which by itself suggests extramedullary versus intramedullary.

probes.q: Name the three things this history is specifically built to uncover.
probes.a: A band-like (girdle) sensory level, bladder or bowel involvement, and the direction the weakness spread (ascending versus descending).

probes.q: Why does finding sphincter involvement change the urgency of a compressive myelopathy case?
probes.a: It indicates the autonomic pathways are already involved, and recovery of sphincter function is particularly sensitive to how quickly decompression is achieved, so its presence pushes this from urgent toward emergency management.

rubric.text: Directly asks about bladder and bowel function
Asks about a band-like sensory sensation
Establishes whether the weakness spread ascending or descending

skill.hx.cord.aetiology.title: The aetiology history
skill.hx.cord.aetiology.oneLine: In this population, ask about tuberculosis before you ask about anything else
skill.hx.cord.aetiology.why: The cause of a compressive myelopathy is often guessable from the history alone, and in an Indian setting tuberculosis of the spine is common enough, and treatable enough, that it must be actively asked about rather than left to imaging to discover.

asks.text: Any known tuberculosis contact, past TB treatment, or symptoms of active TB (cough, fever, night sweats, weight loss)?
Any known cancer, in this patient or their close family, or unexplained weight loss?
Any history of trauma to the back, however minor it seemed at the time?
Any known bleeding disorder or anticoagulant use, relevant to a spontaneous epidural haematoma?

teach.heading: Why tuberculosis is asked about first in this setting
teach.body: Tuberculous (Pott's) spine is a leading cause of compressive myelopathy across age groups here, and unlike most other causes it has a specific, curable medical treatment. A constitutional symptom pattern, low fever, night sweats, weight loss, together with a subacute back pain that has been present for longer than the weakness, is the classic lead-in and is worth actively pursuing rather than waiting for imaging to suggest it.

teach.heading: Other causes worth asking about

points.d: A known primary cancer, or unexplained weight loss and bone pain, raises metastatic cord compression, which is an oncological emergency.
A recent fall or road traffic injury, even one that seemed minor at the time, especially in a patient with pre-existing spondylosis.
Chronic neck or back pain with a slowly progressive course points towards cervical or lumbar spondylotic myelopathy rather than an acute process.
Fever with back pain and a source of bacteraemia, such as a recent skin infection or intravenous drug use, should raise this even though it is less common than the causes above.

teach.note: Asking about all four takes under a minute and often narrows the differential before a single test is ordered.

pitfalls: Not asking about constitutional symptoms or TB contact because the presenting complaint is 'weak legs', not 'cough'.
Assuming malignancy in an older patient without also asking the same TB-focused questions, since the two are not mutually exclusive and can coexist.

probes.q: In an Indian clinical setting, which cause of compressive myelopathy must always be actively asked about?
probes.a: Tuberculosis of the spine (Pott's disease).

skill.exam.cord.spine.title: Examining the spine itself
skill.exam.cord.spine.oneLine: Look, then percuss, before you ever touch a reflex hammer
skill.exam.cord.spine.why: The spine is examined before the neurological exam because a visible deformity or a tender segment can point straight at the level before a single reflex is tested, and because spinal tenderness is one of the features that helps separate an extradural from an intradural lesion.

steps.text: Inspect the whole spine from behind and from the side, specifically looking for a gibbus (a localised angular kyphotic deformity) or any other visible curve or swelling.
Palpate each spinous process for tenderness, and percuss gently down the spine with a closed fist, asking the patient to report any pain and noting exactly where it is.
Inspect and palpate for a paraspinal swelling or abscess.
Assess spinal movement (flexion, extension, lateral bending) only if it can be done safely, and stop immediately if it provokes or worsens neurological symptoms.

skill.exam.cord.spine.normal: A straight spine with no deformity, no tenderness on palpation or percussion, and no paraspinal swelling.
skill.exam.cord.spine.abnormal: A gibbus or other visible deformity; localised tenderness or pain on percussion at a specific level; a paraspinal swelling or abscess.
skill.exam.cord.spine.significance: A gibbus deformity is the classic external sign of tuberculous spinal disease. Localised tenderness at percussion commonly matches the level found on imaging and on the sensory exam, and its presence, together with a symmetrical onset, favours an extradural process over an intradural one.

teach.heading: How to actually examine the spine

points.d: Look from behind and from the side for a visible deformity, a gibbus, or scoliosis, and for any overlying skin change such as a sinus or a hairy patch.
Run a finger down each spinous process feeling for a step or a gap, and press directly over each one for localised tenderness.
A light tap over each spinous process can reproduce pain at the level of the lesion even when palpation alone does not.

teach.note: Do this before the limb examination. A tender or deformed level gives you a level to test against once you move on to sensation and reflexes.

teach.heading: Extradural versus intradural, at the bedside before any scan
teach.note: None of these is individually definitive, but together, symmetrical weakness with spinal tenderness and deformity, they build a reasonable case for an extradural process before imaging confirms it.

pitfalls: Forcing spinal movement testing in a patient with a suspected unstable or actively compressive lesion, which can worsen the deficit.
Skipping spinal percussion because the neurological exam is 'the important part'; it is one of the few bedside clues to extradural versus intradural disease.
Missing a gibbus because the patient was examined only from the front.

probes.q: What is a gibbus, and what does it classically indicate?
probes.a: A localised, angular kyphotic deformity of the spine, classically the external sign of tuberculous (Pott's) spinal disease.

probes.q: A patient has symmetrical leg weakness, spinal tenderness at one level, and a visible deformity there. Does this pattern favour an extradural or an intradural lesion?
probes.a: Extradural: symmetrical onset, spinal tenderness and deformity are all features that favour an extradural process over an intradural one.

rubric.text: Inspects the whole spine for deformity before palpating
Percusses the spine and localises any tenderness to a specific level

skill.hx.pd.title: The Parkinson's history
skill.hx.pd.oneLine: The tremor's own character, and the two questions that find a reversible cause
skill.hx.pd.why: The character of the tremor (rest versus action) and a careful drug history are what separate idiopathic disease from a reversible, drug-induced parkinsonism, and missing either is the commonest reason a treatable cause is overlooked.

asks.text: When is the tremor most noticeable: at rest, or when you are using the hand for something?
Which side did it start on, and has the other side become involved since?
Have you noticed becoming slower at everyday tasks, such as buttoning a shirt, or that your handwriting has become smaller?
Any change in your walking, in your voice, or has anyone commented that your face looks less expressive?
What medicines are you taking now, or have taken in the past year, particularly anything for nausea, vomiting, or a psychiatric condition?
Any fainting or lightheadedness on standing, constipation, or urinary symptoms?
Has anyone else in the family had a tremor or Parkinson's disease?

teach.heading: Rest tremor is the one that matters most here
teach.body:
The classic parkinsonian tremor is present when the limb is fully relaxed and supported, at a frequency of roughly 4 to 6 cycles per second, often described by the patient or observed as a pill-rolling movement of the thumb and fingers.

It characteristically DISAPPEARS with voluntary movement and during sleep, which is the opposite behaviour to an action or intention tremor, and is worth asking about directly since patients often describe the tremor generically without this distinction.

teach.heading: The drug history is not a formality here
teach.body: Dopamine receptor blocking drugs (many antiemetics and antipsychotics), and a handful of other agents, produce a parkinsonism that can be clinically identical to the idiopathic disease, and the most useful single clue is a temporal relationship between starting the drug and the onset of symptoms, plus a SYMMETRICAL onset, which is unusual for idiopathic disease.

pitfalls: Not distinguishing rest tremor from action or intention tremor in the history, and so missing the discriminating feature.
Taking a superficial drug history that misses an antiemetic or antipsychotic started months earlier.
Not asking about non-motor symptoms (autonomic, sleep, mood), which are part of the same disease and matter to the patient as much as the tremor does.

probes.q: What frequency and character is the classic parkinsonian tremor?
probes.a: A 4 to 6 Hz rest tremor, often described as pill-rolling, that improves with voluntary movement and disappears in sleep.

probes.q: Why does the drug history matter so much in a new presentation of parkinsonism?
probes.a: Dopamine receptor blocking drugs (many antiemetics and antipsychotics) can cause a parkinsonism that looks clinically identical to idiopathic disease but is reversible on stopping the drug, and a temporal link to a new medication, especially with symmetrical onset, should raise this possibility.

rubric.text: Establishes whether the tremor is present at rest and improves with action
Takes a specific drug history including antiemetics and antipsychotics

skill.hx.neuropathy.ascending.title: The ascending-weakness history
skill.hx.neuropathy.ascending.oneLine: The infection they forgot, the direction it travelled, and the two questions that flag danger
skill.hx.neuropathy.ascending.why: A preceding infection is easy for a patient to consider irrelevant and not mention, and the specific direction of spread, together with breathing and swallowing difficulty, are what turn a routine neurology history into a safety-critical one.

asks.text: Where did the weakness start, and has it spread since, and in which direction?
Have you had a cold, sore throat, or an episode of diarrhoea in the last few weeks?
Any numbness, tingling, or pain, and if so, where compared with the weakness?
Any difficulty breathing, or does it feel harder to take a deep breath?
Any difficulty swallowing, or has your voice changed?
Any change in your bladder or bowel control?
Any recent vaccination, surgery, or new medication?

teach.heading: The preceding infection is the single most useful question here
teach.body: A history of a gastrointestinal or upper respiratory infection one to three weeks before the weakness began is present in a large proportion of Guillain-Barre syndrome cases, and patients very often will not connect a resolved bout of diarrhoea, weeks earlier, to a new weakness now unless asked about it specifically.

teach.heading: Ascending weakness, and why the direction matters
teach.body: 'Ascending' weakness, first the legs, then the trunk, then the arms, then bulbar and respiratory muscles, is the classic Guillain-Barre pattern and mirrors the book's own worked example. The rarer Miller Fisher variant instead does the opposite, starting with the eye movements and face and descending. Establishing which direction it is travelling, and how fast, tells you how urgently to monitor breathing and swallowing.

teach.heading: Breathing and swallowing are not optional questions
teach.body: Ask about them directly in every suspected case, even a mild one, because respiratory and bulbar involvement can progress over hours and is the reason this diagnosis is followed with serial monitoring rather than a single assessment.

pitfalls: Not asking specifically about a preceding infection, and so missing the single most useful piece of supporting history.
Asking about breathing only once, rather than treating it as something to reassess if the weakness is still progressing.
Assuming a mild presentation cannot progress to respiratory involvement.

probes.q: What preceding event should be actively asked about in any suspected Guillain-Barre syndrome?
probes.a: A gastrointestinal or upper respiratory infection in the preceding one to three weeks.

probes.q: Describe the classic direction of weakness spread in Guillain-Barre syndrome, and name the variant that reverses it.
probes.a: Classically ascending: legs first, then trunk, then arms, then bulbar and respiratory muscles. The Miller Fisher variant instead is descending, starting with eye movements and the face.

rubric.text: Asks specifically about a preceding infection
Asks specifically about breathing and swallowing

skill.hx.cnpalsy.title: The isolated facial palsy history
skill.hx.cnpalsy.oneLine: The three questions that separate Bell's palsy from everything that mimics it
skill.hx.cnpalsy.why: Bell's palsy is diagnosed by having no other explanation, so the history has to actively hunt for the specific things that WOULD explain it: a rash, an ear problem, a systemic disease, or a second neurological sign, before it can be labelled idiopathic.

asks.text: Exactly how did it start, and over how long: sudden, or did it creep in over days or weeks?
Any pain behind or below the ear before the weakness started?
Any rash, blisters, or vesicles in or around the ear, or on the palate?
Any ear discharge, hearing change, or a known ear infection?
Any change in taste, or does sound seem unusually loud on that side?
Any weakness, numbness, or clumsiness anywhere else in the body?
Do you have diabetes, and are you pregnant, if relevant, both of which are recognised associations?
Has this happened before, on either side?

teach.heading: Onset speed is still doing the same job it always does
teach.body: A genuinely sudden onset, noticed within a day, fits an idiopathic or viral-associated palsy or a vascular event; a palsy that has crept in gradually over weeks should make you think much harder about a structural cause, particularly a parotid or cerebellopontine angle tumour, rather than assume Bell's palsy.

teach.heading: A rash changes the diagnosis, not just the severity
teach.body: A vesicular rash in the ear canal, on the pinna, or on the soft palate, together with the facial weakness, is Ramsay Hunt syndrome (herpes zoster oticus), which has a different course and a real risk of hearing loss, and is not the same diagnosis as Bell's palsy even though the facial weakness itself can look identical.

pitfalls: Not asking specifically about a rash, and so missing Ramsay Hunt syndrome.
Not asking about weakness or sensation elsewhere in the body, and so missing a Guillain-Barre syndrome presenting with bilateral, or apparently unilateral, facial weakness.
Accepting 'sudden' without confirming the actual timescale, since a subacute, progressive course changes the differential substantially.

probes.q: What history finding would make you diagnose Ramsay Hunt syndrome rather than Bell's palsy?
probes.a: A vesicular rash in the ear canal, on the pinna, or on the palate, accompanying the facial weakness.

probes.q: Why does a facial palsy that has developed gradually over several weeks need a different level of concern than one that appeared overnight?
probes.a: A slowly progressive course is atypical for Bell's palsy and should prompt active consideration of a structural cause, particularly a parotid gland tumour or a cerebellopontine angle lesion, rather than being assumed idiopathic.

rubric.text: Asks specifically about a vesicular rash
Asks about weakness or sensory change elsewhere in the body

skill.hx.ataxia.title: The ataxia history
skill.hx.ataxia.oneLine: Worse in the dark, and a fall at the wash-basin, are the patient already telling you the type
skill.hx.ataxia.why: Two everyday details, whether the unsteadiness is worse when vision is reduced, and a history of losing balance with the eyes briefly closed during ordinary activities, are close bedside equivalents of Romberg's test and can point strongly toward a sensory cause before you have examined the patient at all.

asks.text: Is the unsteadiness worse in the dark, in dim light, or when walking through a narrow space?
Have you ever lost your balance or fallen while washing your face at the sink, drying your face with a towel, or pulling a shirt over your head, times when your eyes are briefly closed?
Any spinning sensation (vertigo), ringing in the ears, or hearing change?
Any numbness, tingling, or a feeling of walking on cotton wool in the feet?
What is your diet like, particularly how much meat, dairy and eggs you eat, and do you drink alcohol?
What medicines do you take, or have taken for a long period, including any anti-seizure medication?
Any change in speech, swallowing, or double vision?
Is anyone else in the family affected by something similar?

teach.heading: Worse in the dark, and the wash-basin sign, are near-bedside Romberg's tests
teach.body: A sensory ataxia depends on vision to compensate for the lost proprioceptive input, so it characteristically worsens once vision is reduced or removed, in dim light, at night, or in the brief moment the eyes close to wash the face or pull on a shirt. A patient who volunteers a fall at the sink, or difficulty in a dark room, has essentially already described a positive Romberg's sign from their own daily life, before you have formally tested it.

teach.heading: Vertigo, tinnitus and hearing loss point away from the cord and toward the ear
teach.body: These three symptoms travelling together with the unsteadiness point specifically toward a vestibular cause, and their absence is just as informative: a patient with a convincing sensory or cerebellar picture who denies all three has one more reason to look elsewhere for the cause.

teach.heading: Diet, alcohol and drugs are not routine questions here, they are the differential
teach.body: A restrictive diet raises B12 or vitamin E deficiency; alcohol use raises both an acute toxic cerebellar effect and chronic nutritional (B1) causes; specific drugs, phenytoin, lithium and several chemotherapy agents among them, are recognised causes of a cerebellar ataxia in their own right.

pitfalls: Not asking specifically about worsening in the dark or at the wash-basin, and so missing the history-level equivalent of a positive Romberg's test.
Skipping the diet and alcohol history because the presenting complaint is 'unsteady walking' rather than anything obviously nutritional.
Forgetting to ask about vertigo, tinnitus and hearing change as a specific set, rather than a generic 'any ear problems'.

probes.q: A patient describes nearly falling while washing their face with their eyes closed. What type of ataxia does this suggest?
probes.a: Sensory ataxia, since the loss of balance specifically when vision is removed is the wash-basin sign, a bedside equivalent of a positive Romberg's test.

probes.q: Name three things in the history that should be actively asked about because they are recognised causes of a cerebellar ataxia.
probes.a: Alcohol use, specific drugs (phenytoin, lithium, certain chemotherapy agents), and a preceding viral or other infectious illness.

rubric.text: Asks whether the unsteadiness is worse with reduced vision (dark, wash-basin sign)
Asks specifically about vertigo, tinnitus and hearing change
Takes a diet, alcohol and drug history aimed at the differential
